III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00243

The secret of this transformation lies in a transfer of the Witness's act of witnessing, a reversal of roles. When the creature withdraws—or rather, becomes transparent—it is no longer simply a creature looking at God. In and through the creature's gaze, God Himself looks at Himself. Once we grasp this, we already have some idea of what Rûzbehân's religion of love will mean: a love that answers God's self-disclosure through Beauty.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00244

But this is very far from the ordinary state of human consciousness. Most people do not even suspect that there is an ordeal of the Veil. The Veil itself, a blind unawareness, is their accepted “normal” condition. In this way they complete God's estrangement from Himself. To enter into the secret, we must turn to the heart of creation, where we see how completely this understanding of Spirit is centered on prophecy.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00245

Here we encounter the idea of a mystical hierarchy: initiates invisibly dispersed throughout the earth and other worlds. The sources of this idea, and its place in Sufism, still call for much further research. We already know, from the vision that led Rûzbehân to reflect on the hidden meaning of the seven stars of the Great Bear, that he considered himself one of the seven Abdâl of his age.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00246

The highest members of this mysterious hierarchy are those who have triumphed over the ordeal of the Veil. This helps us understand what esoteric theosophy means when it says that the earthly world continues to exist through them, and that without them it could not endure for even an instant.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00247

The acts of creation are divine gazes, divine contemplations (nazarât). This is why we have just read that every particle of being emerging as an individual within the divine Light is an eye (‘ayn) through which that Light contemplates itself. These acts of contemplation bring forth every order of creation, from the angels who bear the Throne to Adam, who is “the eye in which all is gathered” (‘ayn al-jam‘), because all the divine Gazes converge in the Adamic form. Creation, understood as divine contemplation, is not an object separate from the act of contemplating.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00248

Rather, it is the very organ through which contemplation takes place. Every created being is thus a divine eye: nothing can become visible without an organ of sight. In this sense every creature, as a divine eye, is a theophany (tajallî), a manifestation of God. From Adam, the first prophet and a complete theophany, the divine gaze is divided and reflected anew, from Messenger (Rasûl) to Messenger, from prophet (Nabî) to prophet, from friend of God (Walî) to friend of God.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00249

At every period in the cycle of prophecy, there are always 360 persons on earth upon whom the divine Gaze rests (mawâqi‘ al-nazar). They are at the same time the eyes through which God contemplates His creatures and contemplates Himself within them. This also means that they are the eyes through which God makes Himself visible to His creatures.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00250
Notice, in passing, that we have arrived at an essential Shiite idea: the Imam as the Face through which God looks upon humanity and, at the same time, the Face through which humanity looks upon God.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00251

We can see how, in Sunni Sufism, the person of the Imam disappears, yet the place he occupied remains unmistakably marked. Speaking of the “Earth's lament,” Rûzbehân writes: “After our Prophet's death, the Earth complained to God: ‘My God! The prophets and Messengers have passed away. Will no nabî ever again walk upon my soil? Yet I cannot remain without them.’ And God said to her: ‘By My might and My glory!
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00252

“For every nabî and every Messenger (rasûl), I shall create for you a protecting Friend (Walî), until the Day of Resurrection.’” Is this not precisely the Shiite idea that every prophet is succeeded by his Imam? After the mission of the last Prophet brought the “cycle of prophecy” to its close, the “cycle of walâyat”—the spiritual guardianship of God's friends—began. Each of the friends of God in this latter cycle occupies a rank corresponding to that of a prophet in the earlier cycle.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00253

Where could the idea of this protecting Friend, who succeeds the Prophet until the Resurrection, have come from, if not from the Shiite understanding of the Imam? The Imam is the keystone of the mystical hierarchy Rûzbehân now describes: the beings who, generation after generation, are the eyes through which God looks upon the world and through which the world looks upon God.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00254

In these mysterious figures, the innermost heart of each being corresponds to the heart of the theophany of the divine Names, Attributes, and Essence. They are at once the eyes through which God appears to His creatures and those through which He contemplates them. They are like a mirror struck by sunlight, reflecting that light outward upon this world and other worlds.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00255

“God possesses on Earth three hundred eyes, or persons (‘ayn), whose hearts correspond to Adam's heart; forty whose hearts correspond to Moses' heart; seven whose hearts correspond to Abraham's heart; five whose hearts correspond to Gabriel's heart; three whose hearts correspond to Michael's heart; and one whose heart corresponds to Seraphiel's heart.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00256

That solitary one, whose heart corresponds to Seraphiel's, is the mystical pole of the world. Once again, how can we fail to recognize here the spiritual rank that Shiism assigns to the Imam—now the “Hidden Imam,” the “Seal of Muhammadan walâyat”? Are we not confronted, inevitably, with an “Imamology that dares not speak its name”?
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00257

On the other hand, transferring the Imam's prerogative to someone else dislocates not only the whole structure of the doctrine of the Imam, but the structure of the doctrine of prophecy as well. This is one reason why Shiism, as the esoteric dimension of Islam, has reservations about certain forms of Sufism.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00258
Yet it is true that one of Rûzbehân's visions, discussed earlier, explicitly names the First Imam as the source of walâyat.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00259

We have already spoken several times of the mystical hierarchy itself, and shall return to it again (see Book I above). The details of its ranks vary considerably; this is not the place to attempt a comprehensive account. We need only note that the hadîth just quoted by Rûzbehân—which itself exists in different versions—lists a total of 356 persons. Four further figures are ordinarily added: Christ, Khezr, Elijah, and Idris (Enoch, identified with Hermes).
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00260

This brings the number to 360. Each of these 360 persons represents, or corresponds to, one of the 360 divine Names. Every Name is rooted in an Attribute of the divine Essence; it is also the proper name of a divine activity, the act of self-disclosure that reveals that Attribute as a created being, an eye through which God contemplates Himself or contemplates that Attribute.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00261

The number 360 is also connected with the image of the celestial sphere divided into 360 degrees, by which the full cycle of day and night is measured. Likewise, according to a saying attributed to the Prophet, “Every day and every night God casts 360 gazes. With each gaze He creates and provides, gives life and gives death, takes away the means of being and grants the means to sustain existence.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00262

“Every gaze, at every hour of day and night, is directed toward an eye among His eyes”—God looks upon His own eyes—“and not toward the profane world (donyâ, the world whose eyes are turned only upon itself). For that world God has never looked upon since Creation, holding it in abhorrence.” In other words, that world has never looked toward Him, and so could not become the divine gaze that would look upon it. At most, the world declares that God “does not look at it”—meaning that God is no concern of its own.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00263

Thus God looks upon the world through beings unknown to the unseeing mass of humanity. As His creatures, they are the eyes through which God contemplates Himself; equally, they are the eyes through which His creation contemplates Him. They are the eyes of their age. Adam, for example, was the eye of his age (‘ayn zamânihi), the theophany of his time.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00264

At the heart of this teaching we find the remarkable persistence of a single fundamental insight, appearing again and again among mystics as different as Rûzbehân and Meister Eckhart. Eckhart expresses it in his celebrated formula: the eye with which I know God is the very eye with which God knows me.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00265

This is what it means for a creature to be God's eye. It is the secret of the theophanies that fill Rûzbehân's life, and the secret by which the mystic triumphs over the ordeal of the Veil: he resolves the ambiguity inherent in everything that becomes manifest. Recognizing his own existence as the gaze through which God contemplates Himself, he becomes the organ through which God looks upon the world at every hour of day and night. This is why we have spoken here of a phenomenology of Spirit.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00266

For if that gaze were to close, if those beings who are the divine Gaze through which God knows the world ceased to exist, the world itself would collapse. This is what all the Sufi theosophers mean when they say that without the complete company of these beings—unknown to the multitude, sustained by their “pole,” whom Shiites identify with the Hidden Imam—earthly life could not continue for a single instant.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00267

Something far greater is at stake than any “social role” our age might still be willing to acknowledge in people of the spirit. This is a function of cosmic salvation. Each mystic, over the course of a spiritual life, becomes connected with one or another of these mysterious figures, as do the disciples of Khezr. Through that figure, and by becoming like him, the mystic becomes the gaze through which God contemplates Himself, His witness of contemplation.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00268

Yet Rûzbehân gives us no grounds for thinking that victory over the ordeal of the Veil confers lasting security. The divine Essence must remain forever inaccessible: it can be approached only through the theophanies at the different levels of existence, and through the beings who are their eyes. There is a Veil for the Angel to overcome, a Veil for the prophets, a Veil for the Awliyâ, a Veil for each rank of the mystical hierarchy, for every degree of spiritual attainment, for every step along the Way. Here too Rûzbehân's analysis is remarkably penetrating.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00269

In short, the Veil in every case is the act of looking away from what the theophany reveals, and attending instead to the one who sees it, considered in isolation, and to that person's own experiences. It is the temptation to settle into a state of repose whose effect would be the opposite of the command, “O soul at peace, return to your Lord.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00270

As Abû Yazîd Bastâmî says, even the sweetness of love, the purity of devotion, and spiritual gifts themselves can become a Veil. The creature becomes opaque when it stops at its own nonbeing—the nothingness of its pretensions and ignorance. The world loses its transparency and sets itself up as an Other facing God, an Other upon which not even God can look. Rûzbehân returns to the point with striking insistence.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00271

God has never looked at this world devoid of transparency since its creation, for He can look only upon His own eyes, which look toward Him. How then could He see this world, when it has no eyes and does not see Him? But no spiritual rank is exempt from the ordeal of the Veil. Every prophet has encountered it, endured it, and overcome it in his own way. Each Veil, each ordeal, corresponds to a particular spiritual station or dwelling place.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00272
What is a veil for the advanced mystic may be the furthest point a beginner (morîd) can possibly reach.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00273

An incident involving a disciple of Abû Torâb Najashî makes this clear. The disciple was a young man with an exceptional capacity for ecstasy and a high spiritual state. He laid claim to numerous spiritual stations (maqâmât) and states of mystical experience (ahwâl). Again and again his master would say to him, “My friend, if only you could see Abû Yazîd Bastâmî!” One day the disciple lost his temper.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00274

“I see the God of Abû Yazîd,” he declared. “I have no need of Abû Yazîd.” His master replied, “Poor boy! You see God with your own eye. If you saw Abû Yazîd, you would see God with Abû Yazîd's eye.” The disciple was astonished. “You are right!” he said. “Get up, and let us go to him.” The master rose, and they set out to find Abû Yazîd.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00275

When they reached him, Abû Yazîd was just emerging from a grove, wearing a fur coat turned inside out. The young man looked at him, cried out, and fell lifeless to the ground. Abû Yazîd gently shook him and said in Persian, “Poor child! You could not bear to see God!” Abû Torâb asked him, “My lord, does everyone who sees you die?” “Certainly not,” Abû Yazîd answered.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00276

“But there was a secret within your disciple, and that secret had not revealed itself to him as he wished. When he saw me, it was disclosed to him; he could not bear it, and he died, because he was weak.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00277

The story, whose mysterious psychology is somewhat illuminated by what we have just discussed, teaches us how dangerous mystical experience can be when the many different degrees and paths are ignored. Because the mystic's contemplation is itself the act by which God contemplates him, it would be perilous—or rather, impossible—for one person to force another into the same form or the same level of contemplation.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00278

Curiously, we can again see in this story a transformation of the Shiite idea of the Imam, who, as Imam, is the shâhid, the Witness through whom God looks and through whom the mystic looks upon his God, within God's own gaze upon him. Here, in the absence of the Imam, Abû Yazîd took his place.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00279
But the young disciple died of it.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00280

Finally, a visionary account handed down by the celebrated Sufi of Baghdad, Jonayd (originally from Nehâvand in Iran, tenth century), shows us in the language of actual spiritual experience how creation as the “eye of God” is bound up with the ordeal of the Veil, and what it means, in a theophany, for the gaze “not to swerve.” The central figure is Jonayd's own master, the equally renowned Sufi Sarî al-Saqatî. One day Jonayd was with him in the company of several friends when the master suddenly passed into ecstasy.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00281

When he came to himself, he was surrounded by a light so intense that it dazzled everyone around him. Then he began to tell them what had happened. He had been snatched away from the circle of his friends and carried upward from heaven to heaven. He had passed through Veils of dazzling light: first the Veil of Beauty, then the Veil of Majesty, then the Veil of Condensation (motakâthifa, whose nature he could not describe), and finally the Veil of Power.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00282

There, overcome with awe and filled with both fear and longing, he understood that he stood before the Divine Being. From behind that Veil came a call: “O Sarî!” At the sound of the voice he felt as though his limbs were breaking and his joints coming apart.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00283

But God “gathered him together” and addressed him a second time: “O Sarî! Do you know how My creation exists together with Me (kayfa khalqî ma‘î)?” The divine Voice then recalled the mysterious scene of the covenant made before time, which we encountered earlier: “Am I not your Lord?” To the Spirits who had acclaimed Him, God showed the grace and beauty of the earthly world.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00284

Nine-tenths went toward it; one-tenth remained. To those who remained, God showed paradise with all its delights and joys. Nine-tenths chose it; one-tenth remained. To these God then showed hell with all its torments and humiliations. Nine-tenths fled; one-tenth remained. The successive tests continued. Each time, of those who had persevered, nine-tenths fell away.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00285

God subjected them to the ordeal of Experience, under which nine-tenths were broken; to the ordeal of love, before which nine-tenths took fright; to the Veil of Nearness, in whose light nine-tenths were consumed; and to the Veil of overwhelming Majesty (hayba, the tremendum), beneath which nine-tenths were submerged. After these seven ordeals, each leaving only a tenth of those who had survived the last, God revealed the Veil of Power to the final remnant. They stood before it, amazed and stunned.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00286

At this point the divine account, which Sarî heard spoken in the first person during his ecstasy, takes on a dramatic force in which the whole experience of these Sufis reaches its height: “I called to them, congratulated them, and clothed them in the lights of Power. ‘O My faithful ones!’ I said. They answered: ‘Here we are, our Lord, our Prince!’
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00287

“I said: ‘I showed you the earthly world. Some went toward it, but you remained. I showed you paradise. Some chose it, but you remained. I showed you hell. Some fled, but you remained. I tested you with the Ordeal. Some were broken, but you were not. I revealed to you the ordeal of love. Some were afraid, but you did not turn away.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00288

“I lifted for you the Veil of Nearness. Some grew proud, but I kept you tranquil. I lifted for you the Veil of overwhelming Majesty. Some went beyond it, but you came to a halt. I lifted for you the Veil of Power, and you remained before it, astonished and dazzled, for I had made you steadfast. What, then, do you want? What are you seeking?’
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00289

“‘We want only You. We seek nothing but You. You are our goal.’ ‘O My faithful ones! You are exposing yourselves to the ordeal that has destroyed countless others before you, world after world, more than anyone but I can number, before the time of your father Adam, from age upon age and into eternity upon eternity. Torment was foretold for them.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00290

“Only those who know have knowledge of it. Between Me and you there lies one of My torments, which no one can endure, a torment that grows ever more intense. The hardest rock could not bear it, nor can human beings withstand it.’ ‘Our Prince, our Lord! Is it You Yourself who will lay this torment upon us?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘That is enough for us.’
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00291

“Then I said to them: ‘Now I know that you are the sincere ones, true in the very truth of your seeking. Now I set you free: I make you the vessels of My Knowledge, the dwelling places of My secret. It is through Me that you speak; you are those who call others toward Me.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00292

“I am yours and you are Mine. I share My secrets with you and you share your secrets with Me. You are the initiates into the mysteries, the intimate companions, those who belong within the kingdom; you are the pure-hearted intimates.’ ‘Then make known what you have received from Me, O Sarî, My creature. Truly, I am the Subtle, the All-Knowing.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00293

“Understand through Me, make known what you have heard from Me, and be forgiving and merciful toward My faithful ones.’” Having passed on the account he received from his master after the latter emerged from ecstasy, Jonayd adds: “I never spoke of this account until after the shaykh had departed this world. If I have added anything to it or left anything out, may God forgive me.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00294

After recounting this vision in full, Rûzbehân adds: “I have cited this sublime vision so that the contemplative may meditate upon it ... so that he may understand what the Veils and Unveilings are on the path to the highest mystical knowledge, and grasp what we mean when we speak of the clouding (ighâna) that occurs even at the spiritual station of love and attainment.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00295

“For through this God has made known to us that in the hearts of those who belong to the hidden world (ahl al-ghayba) there is both veiling and theophany. Even the hearts of the gnostics (‘arifîn), those who know God, cannot escape these until they reach their goal: the unveiling of the vision of vision (kashf ‘iyân al-‘iyân) in the contemplation of the Merciful. This is the ordeal reserved for the spiritual family of those who truly know the ordeal of the Veil.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00296

“Do you not see how He tested them in the account the Shaykh (Sarî) gave of his mi‘râj, his ascent through the heavens? God subjected them to the torments of the Veil as an ordeal reserved especially for them, that they might burn with the fire of longing in the station of separation. Sarî al-Saqatî himself had sought refuge in God, his innermost consciousness (sirr) taking flight toward Him, when he said: ‘Whatever punishment You wish to inflict on me, do not cast me into the misery of the Veil.’
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00297

“One of them said: ‘The impossibility of reaching Him is worse than death.’” To triumph over this ordeal, we may say, is also to escape the “madness of the unattainable,” the despair of never reaching one's goal. Why is this? What brought about the wonderful reversal in Sarî al-Saqatî's “dialogue in heaven”—“I am yours and you are Mine.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00298

“I share My secrets with you and you share your secrets with Me”—was that, each time the ordeal returned with greater force, those who held firm never let their gaze swerve. Others allowed themselves to be distracted by what was offered to them; they contemplated “something other than You.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00299

But those who held firm, amid beauty and torment, fulfillment and abandonment, saw only You—even while, in the very act of attaining You, they suffered the anguish of Your inaccessibility. Here lies the whole secret of the faithful lover: one must neither turn away from human beauty nor turn toward it as an end in itself. One must keep one's gaze straight, “neither swerving nor overstepping”: not swerving from what human beauty reveals, and not overstepping the dignity of that beauty as a creature, whose task is to reveal God.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00300

The clouding occurs when one sees only the outward appearance; it awakens the divine jealousy that refuses to be seen. To see what is inward and invisible is to see the gaze of God that the creature itself is, to become the very eye of that gaze. This is the “vision of vision” (‘iyân al-‘iyân), the highest attainment. It frees God from His jealousy: “I am yours and you are Mine.” To become the eye through which God sees Himself is to realize esoteric tawhîd.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00301

By contrast, the outward believer's attitude—an abstract monotheism that posits a transcendent God and imagines it glorifies Him by worshipping from the outside—ultimately comes close to that of the unbeliever who is captivated by visible appearances. Both confuse holûl with tajallî: incarnation with theophany.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00302

“Oh, what a little child,” cries Rûzbehân, “whoever sees the Moon above a mountain peak and imagines that by climbing to the summit he will be able to seize it! How could he lay hold of it, when the Moon lies beyond the Veil of Mount Qâf, the cosmic mountain? ... I contemplated the new Moon of Unity, but a jealousy older than time raised a cloud and kept me from reaching it.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00303

“So I remained between the two, between separation and reunion, with nowhere to flee and no refuge where I could weep. ... I wrote this book at the dictation of a wounded consciousness and a wounded heart, and sealed it with the inspirations born of my ordeal—in the presence of the Merciful.”
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00304

From childhood, when he first received the “touches of God,” until his death, Rûzbehân lived through this continual movement: from joy before a vision of the Beloved recognized in His image, to the torment of an unattainable presence felt even in the moment of attainment.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00305

Let us return to some pages of the “Journal” of his visions. What predominates there is an enchanted joy before faces of heavenly beauty—a beauty that can disclose itself only to someone whose gaze is so pure that it becomes the very organ of divine vision, the “vision of vision.” At other moments, however, he becomes conscious of a fear that he may be betraying the sharî‘at, Islamic religious law, and the constraint imposed by outward tawhîd: no tashbîh, no symbolic likeness between God and created things!
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00306

Yet if one observes tanzîh, refusing to attribute any qualities of created beings to the divine, how can one ever bear witness: “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms”? This contradiction will be overcome in the mystical experience of human love—or rather, in the very essence of divine love as it is tasted in the form of human love, as understood by the Sufism of the Faithful of Love.
III. The Clouding of the Heart and the Ordeal of the Veil
passage-en-00307

To understand how the two dwell within one another, how divine peace likewise dwells within human restlessness, we must become acquainted with the horizons that open before Rûzbehân's consciousness—or, more precisely, his consciousness beyond ordinary consciousness—the figures that inhabit it, and the beings of heavenly beauty whose companionship he shares.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00308
Chapter IV Diarium spirituale
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00309

After recording the first events of his spiritual autobiography in his “Journal”—whose title, The Unveiling of Secrets (Kashf al-asrâr), is by no means a mere figure of speech—Ruzbihan describes the visions of his childhood and adolescence. He then declares:
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00310

“Afterwards, the doors were opened to me of the sciences inspired by God (‘olûm ladonîya): knowledge of hidden and subtle realities, and of mysteries before which even learned men stand bewildered. Then I found that certain prayers of mine had been answered, and that I had been granted certain miraculous gifts. My secret consciousness (sirr, or ‘transconsciousness,’ the innermost mystery of the soul) became established in the realities beyond the senses (haqâ’iq), and I began to ascend the degrees of the mystical ladder. I experienced the spiritual stations (maqâmât), the passing states of the soul (ahwâl), revelations (moshâkafât), and the higher knowledge of divine unity (tawhîd).
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00311
“In short, through countless discoveries of the invisible worlds, I journeyed into the enchanted regions of the heart.”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00312

The visions and revelations recorded throughout this Diarium are no longer arranged chronologically once the episodes of his early youth have been recounted. Instead, certain themes emerge with extraordinary force. Particular visions, figures, confidences, and prayers recur so insistently that, as we read, we begin almost unconsciously to group them according to their subjects. What this exceptional document discloses to us, in some measure, are the archetypal figures that dominate the consciousness of an Iranian Sufi—and, through him, the consciousness of his entire spiritual family.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00313

We can mention only a very small number of these visions here, but they may at least suggest their importance for a general understanding of visionary consciousness among mystics. Our attention will be directed especially to the scenes of encounter in which the subtle reality of the “world of Mystery” takes on the vivid, tangible forms of gentle beings inhabiting an enchanted heavenly Earth: visions of the prophets, the angels, and the paradises. Above all, we shall consider those repeated encounters in which a contradiction that reason cannot resolve seems to dissolve: the transcendent, inaccessible God appears as the eternal Companion of the soul in love. For a Shiite mystic, that Companion would be his Imam.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00314

But without a theology of the Imam, the loving soul cannot simply forget what official theology has taught it. Even in moments of peace, it remains troubled. Yet this very unease gives rise to a visionary initiation through which the conflict itself disappears.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00315

“And I saw, in the world of Mystery, a universe illuminated by a radiant Light. I saw God (al-Haqq, the Real) clothed in Majesty, Grace, and Beauty. He gave me to drink from the sea of divine affection (wadâd), raised me to the station of intimacy, and showed me the holy world (‘âlam al-Qods).
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00316

“After I had travelled through the expanse of pre-eternity, I came to rest at the Threshold of Power. There I saw all the prophets assembled. I saw Moses holding the Torah, Jesus holding the Gospel, David holding the Book of Psalms, and Muhammad holding the Quran. Then Moses let me taste the Torah; Jesus let me taste the Gospel; David let me taste the Psalter; and Muhammad let me taste the Quran.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00317

“But Adam gave me to drink of the ‘Most Beautiful Names of God,’ together with the Supreme Name. Then I understood as much as I was permitted to understand of the higher knowledge of divine wisdom—the knowledge with which God has set his seal upon his prophets and his Friends (Awliyâ’) (§ 32).”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00318

Another vision of the prophets gives Ruzbihan an opportunity to clarify one of his characteristic technical expressions. It also begins to show us the place that Abraham will occupy among the prophets of the religion of love.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00319

“I saw Abraham among certain mountains, where the light was rising from the star of the divine acts of manifestation (af‘âl), which are the Mirror in which the Essence and Attributes become visible (mir’ât tajallî). Abraham was searching for God and saying: ‘This is my Lord’ (Quran 6:76–78). Then I saw an imposing shaykh descending from a mountain. His eyes blazed with an awe-inspiring majesty. His hair was whiter than snow. I understood that it was Moses coming down from Sinai (§ 67).”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00320

This vision is followed by a vision of angels that displays the characteristic features of Ruzbihan’s angelology. In his state of ecstasy, he recalls the world of the malakût, the heavenly realm of the angels:
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00321

“And behold, that world revealed itself openly to me. I saw the Angels of the Spirit (Rûhânîyûn), the Angels of Divine Lordship (Rabbânîyûn), the Angels of Holiness (Qodsîyûn), the Angels of Majesty (Jalâlîyûn), and the Angels of Beauty (Jamâlîyûn), all seated together. Their robes were like those of brides, more beautiful than anything I had ever seen. Before me I saw the two angels called the ‘Noble Scribes’ (Quran 82:11), and they seemed to be in love with me.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00322

“In the foremost rank of their assembly I saw Gabriel, like a bride, like the moon among the stars. His hair resembled that of women, arranged in very long braids. He wore a red robe embroidered in green. He wept because of me, out of longing for me. And all the angels likewise passed their time in the sweetness of looking upon me, as though they longed for me and rejoiced in my spiritual state (§ 68).”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00323

This loving emotion, these feminine features, recur throughout Ruzbihan’s visions of angels. They belong to an absolute Feminine, since—as the Hurufis would later insist—they are shared by the young woman and the adolescent boy.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00324

“Another time, I saw God bearing the attributes of Majesty and Beauty. With him were angels resembling extraordinarily beautiful women, whose braided hair fell all the way to the ground. I said: ‘O my God! How will you take possession of my spirit at the moment of my death?’ He answered: ‘I shall come to you from the depths of pre-eternity. I shall take your spirit in my hand, like this, and carry it to the dwelling of intimacy.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00325

“I shall give you the wine of Nearness to drink, and I shall show you my Beauty and Majesty as you desire, without any veil.’ Then I saw Gabriel, Michael, Seraphiel, and Azrael, all dressed in robes of light so beautiful that I cannot describe them. Then I saw Munkar and Nakir, appearing as two handsome, graceful youths. They were playing the rebec beside my tomb and saying to me: ‘We are in love with you. This is how we shall come to meet you in your grave.’ And then every fear vanished from me (§ 37).”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00326

The mystic who thus received a vision in advance of that perilous passage had already, in effect, answered the summons: “O soul at peace, return…” One striking feature of these visionary landscapes is their colour. Red predominates, but it is a red inseparable from the colour of flowers.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00327

“Many times I saw God among cradles of roses, beneath veils of roses, in a universe of red roses and white roses. Often he showered me with roses, pearls, and hyacinths. Often I was allowed to drink with him the wine of the houris, in the Holy Dwelling (§ 39).”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00328

This red is also spontaneously associated with the mystical perception of blood being shed. Ruzbihan senses its meaning in advance, but ambiguously: it inspires both fear and hope. It seems linked, moreover, to the idea of a “martyrdom” undergone in vision, at the very point where Ruzbihan knows, somewhere in his unconscious mind, that he is transgressing the Law—the doctrine of divine unity upheld by literalist theologians. This is suggested first by the prophetic motif of seeing God “in the most beautiful of forms,” and then by the frenzy of love in which the rules governing tashbîh and ta‘tîl are forgotten. These name the two dangers that theology seeks to avoid: making God resemble created beings by attributing their qualities to him, or, at the opposite extreme, reducing him to an abstraction.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00329

“And behold, I saw him in my dwelling, bearing the attributes of Majesty and Beauty, in the most beautiful of forms… I felt a longing, a love, a desire, each intensifying the others. During my ecstasy, the whole question of tashbîh and ta‘tîl was banished from my heart, because in His presence all the standards of intellect and knowledge collapse. Some time passed. Then I saw Him again, rising from the world of Mystery with the attribute of Majesty.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00330

“For several hours I remained immersed in ecstasy. Then I saw Him at dawn. He appeared in Majesty and Beauty in the solitudes of Mystery, at the very threshold of the Place of Mystery, painting the streaks of the eternal dawn with the blood of the Abdâl—the hidden saints. I said to myself: ‘What am I beside them? Could I possibly be one of their number?’
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00331

“At that moment I saw a hue still more subtle than theirs, above their own, and He indicated to me that it was my blood. Then I was seized by an ecstasy of joy. Again and again I cried out. My secret consciousness (sirr), my heart, my intelligence, and my spirit were on the verge of taking flight into the expanse of the divine Selfhood (howîya) and being annihilated in the lights of Mystery.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00332

“Yet I was afraid that what I saw might have to be understood as a trial. For in an earlier vision He had shown Himself slaughtering me and pouring out my blood into the streams of Mystery, and afterwards I had passed through a terrible ordeal. Then I cried: ‘I take refuge in you against You’ (L. 155a).”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00333
The earlier vision to which Ruzbihan alludes is described by him in these words:
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00334

“One night I was contemplating the Place of Mystery. There were what looked like empty streams. Suddenly God seized me and cut my throat. A great quantity of blood flowed from my neck, and soon all the streams were filled with it.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00335

“But behold, my blood took on the appearance of the rays of the sun at dawn, when the sun seems greater than the whole expanse of heaven and earth. And multitudes of angels took my blood and painted their faces with it (§ 28).”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00336

Among these angelic companies, the four figures known in Islamic esotericism as the “Bearers of the Throne” acquire a particularly vivid presence in Ruzbihan’s visions, as we have already observed. Three of them have an even more personal relationship with him, as the following two accounts show.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00337

“The hosts of angels came forth from the depths of Mystery. Their leaders—Gabriel, Michael, and Seraphiel—appeared as young pages, their hair braided like that of women. Then God showered me with roses and pearls. The prophets (Nabî) and the angels did the same. Our Prophet spoke to me and kissed me on the face. After him, Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and all the prophets kissed me in the same way. Then God pronounced blessings upon Muhammad and his prophets and praised them.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00338

“Afterwards He said: ‘I have chosen my servant Ruzbihan for eternal happiness, for the station of one of my Friends (walâyat), and for the investiture of my miraculous gifts. I have made him the vessel of my knowledge and my secrets… He is my representative (khalifa) in this world and in the worlds. Whoever loves him, I love; whoever is his enemy is my enemy’ (§ 49).”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00339
The other account runs as follows:
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00340

“It appeared to me that I was in the Sacred Mosque at Mecca (al-masjid al-harâm). I saw the Prophet, who seemed to be in a state of ecstasy. He was walking around the Kaaba and was near the Black Stone, on its left side. Gabriel stood beneath the portico, near the gate of Safa. Michael stood beside him, and Seraphiel beside them both, while a group of angels stood in the courtyard of the sanctuary.
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00341

“I approached the Prophet, overwhelmed with wonder. He turned towards me and called me by my name. Then each of the three angels—Gabriel, Michael, and Seraphiel—approached me in turn and addressed me by name: ‘O Ruzbihan!’ All three were in ecstasy. Then they drew near to the Prophet, and it seemed to me that the Kaaba itself began to move and came closer to them. Then I danced with them. God made Himself visible to them, and I was there among them, sharing their ecstasy of love and tasting a profound peace (§ 52).”
IV. Diarium spirituale
passage-en-00342

Among these three archangels, Gabriel acquires a particularly striking significance. This is connected with his role in Islamic teachings about prophecy, upon which the mystical experience is modelled. The mystic experiences the Angel of Revelation as his own personal Holy Spirit, as the figure of the divine Other Self. One night, Ruzbihan receives a revelation of the Night of Destiny (laylat al-Qadr):
